title: URL Shortener
summary: Build a read-heavy service that turns long URLs into short codes and redirects at scale.
narrative:
A URL shortener looks trivial and is secretly a masterclass in scale. Writes are rare — someone creates a short link now and then. Reads are enormous — every click on every shortened link, forever, is a lookup that must resolve in milliseconds.

That lopsided read/write ratio drives the whole design. You want a datastore that scales reads horizontally, a cache to serve the hottest links from memory, and an app tier behind a load balancer to glue it together. Clients should never touch the datastore directly.

Wire up the read path so a redirect hits the cache first and falls back to the store, and keep the write path clean. A Bloom filter can cheaply reject codes that were never issued.

functional: Create a short code for a long URL
Redirect a short code to its original URL
Serve the hottest links from cache
nonFunctional: Redirects resolve in under 50 ms at p99
constraints: Clients enter through the load balancer only
The datastore is reachable only from the app tier
specs.tradeoff: A cache-aside layer trades occasional stale reads and added complexity for dramatically lower datastore load.
specs.bonus: Add a Bloom Filter so lookups for codes that were never issued skip the datastore entirely.

missions.label: Add a Cache for hot redirects
Add a NoSQL Database for the mappings
Route clients to the Load Balancer
Fall back to the Database on a miss

topologyRules.message: Traffic must enter through the Load Balancer.
Clients must never reach the datastore directly.
Datastore access must pass through the application tier.

resilienceRules.message: Run at least two Web Servers so a redirect never depends on a single instance.
Front the datastore with a Cache to protect it from the read flood.

hints: The read path is what matters: Client → Load Balancer → Web Server → Cache, with the NoSQL Database behind the cache.
Connect the Web Server to BOTH the Cache and the Database — cache first, database on a miss.
Add a second Web Server to remove the single point of failure, and wire the Cache to the Database so they're companions.
